title: Exploring Adaptive Teaching
author: Shaun Allison
summary: Shaun Allison unpacks the concept of adaptive teaching, distinguishing it carefully from traditional 'differentiation' — arguing that adaptive teaching is a responsive, real-time adjustment to what students are actually showing in the moment, rather than a set of pre-planned differentiated activities or permanent ability groupings. Drawing on the new EEF Inclusive Teaching Guidance, Allison presents a two-part model: universal approaches that benefit all students (especially those with additional needs) and adaptations or additional support deployed strategically when universal approaches alone are insufficient. The article identifies five key universal approaches backed by evidence: explicit instruction, cognitive load management, scaffolding, collaborative learning, and responsive questioning. Allison connects adaptive teaching to the Durrington Teaching Principles in Practice framework and shows how the concept sits within the broader move toward evidence-informed, inclusive pedagogy. The piece is most useful for school leaders developing a coherent instructional model and for teachers who want to understand what responsive teaching looks like in practice, as distinct from paperwork-heavy differentiation plans.
points: The critical conceptual move is distinguishing adaptive teaching from differentiation: adaptive teaching is responsive and occurs in real time based on what students demonstrate, not through pre-planned ability-specific materials.

The EEF two-part model (universal approaches + strategic adaptations) reframes inclusion as something built into high-quality teaching for everyone, not a parallel system for students with additional needs.

Universal approaches — explicit instruction, cognitive load management, scaffolding, collaborative learning, responsive questioning — are powerful precisely because they reduce barriers for all students, not just those identified for support.

The Durrington Teaching Principles framework gives adaptive teaching institutional grounding, showing how responsive practice can be systematized across a school rather than left to individual teacher variation.

The most important practical implication is that adaptive teaching requires skilled observation and decision-making during lessons, not advance planning of differentiated materials — which means professional development needs to focus on in-the-moment responsiveness.
quotes: Over recent years, adaptive teaching has become one of the most frequently used phrases in education. It appears in policy documents, professional development programmes, Ofsted discussions and research literature.

Instead, adaptive teaching describes what highly effective teachers have always done: gathering evidence about learning and using that information to make precise adjustments to instruction so that all pupils can successfully access ambitious curriculum content. The Education Endowment Foundation’s new Guide to Inclusive Teaching [ ] reinforces this understanding.

Responsiveness to Evidence of Learning Teachers actively seek information about what pupils know, understand and can do through questioning, assessment, feedback and observation. They then use this evidence to inform instructional decisions.

High-quality adaptive teaching therefore sits at the intersection of both How Do Our Teaching PiPs Support Adaptive and Inclusive Teaching? The Durrington Teaching Principles in Practice (TPiPs) provide the mechanism through which adaptive and inclusive teaching happens in classrooms every day.
Teachers gain reliable information about readiness for new learning. This reflects the EEF’s emphasis on establishing strong universal classroom routines that support participation for all pupils.

Instruction responds to specific learning needs rather than broad assumptions. This reflects the EEF’s argument that effective adaptations should be informed by ongoing assessment and linked directly to learning needs.

Gathering Responses Mini whiteboards, hinge questions and other response systems provide real-time data. Teachers can then decide whether to: Re-teach a concept Provide another example Increase challenge Add a scaffold Offer further guided practice This exemplifies the EEF’s recommendation that adaptations should often involve increasing the intensity of high-quality teaching rather than changing its fundamental nature.
